subject: future
topic: The 'productivity paradox' shows digital tools are increasing task-switching costs
angle: While cognitive load and specific task types can impair movement control and create switch costs that last for minutes, the number of tasks being supervised does not influence switch costs, and there is no definitive evidence linking subjective cognitive failures to switching performance.
title: The True Cost of Switching

hooks.text: Does your multitasking actually cost you more than you think?
You assume more tasks mean higher costs. The evidence says otherwise.
You are paying a price for every switch you make.
A cursor blinks on a blank screen.
48% of movement control is lost under cognitive load.

reveal.headline: The number of tasks you supervise does not increase switch costs.
reveal.body: Research shows that the quantity of tasks being supervised does not influence the cost of switching between them. This evidence is mixed regarding the link between subjective cognitive failure and performance.

explain.headline: Cognitive load affects movement, not just thought.
explain.body: High cognitive load makes it harder to predictively control your movements. When you switch between different task actions, you are slower than when performing the same task.

matters.headline: The cost of switching is not immediate.
matters.body: A switch cost may last for between 20 seconds and 5 minutes. That may be why you feel a lingering lag after moving between different types of work.

example.headline: A quiet office at 3 p.m.
example.body: You close a spreadsheet and open a video call. You sit for a few moments, staring at the screen before your hands move to type again.

verdict: The evidence shows that cognitive load and specific task environments impact switching and movement control, but the relationship between subjective cognitive failure and switching is not established.
caveat: The research is limited by a lack of definitive evidence connecting subjective cognitive failure to objective switching performance and a lack of consensus on respiratory variability as a reliable index of cognitive load.
caption:
The productivity paradox suggests digital tools increase the cost of switching between tasks. 

Evidence shows that cognitive load impacts movement control and creates switch costs lasting up to 5 minutes, but the number of tasks supervised does not influence these costs. Research is limited by a lack of definitive evidence connecting subjective cognitive failure to objective performance.
